title: Trading US Corporate Bonds: It Pays to Be Flexible | Dimensional
gist: A Dimensional study of 159 million trades across 29,032 US corporate bonds finds that even after years of falling trading costs, similar bonds still trade at widely different effective spreads. Swapping high-cost bonds for low-cost substitutes matched on credit quality, duration and mid-yield added roughly 20 bps of net return per three-month holding period from 2013 to 2024, with gross returns essentially identical.

themes.theme: Cost dispersion in corporate bond trading

insights.claim: US corporate bonds show large dispersion in trading costs between otherwise similar bonds because they trade infrequently and at wider spreads than government bonds, and that dispersion has persisted even as average trading costs declined.
insights.speaker: Aabbhas Garg, Researcher
insights.so_what: Execution quality, not just security selection, is a live source of return in credit portfolios; screen candidate bonds on spread cost before buying.
insights.quote: while trading costs have fallen over time, sizable cost dispersion remains between similar bonds
insights.locator: In our recent paper, using 159 million trades

insights.claim: Dimensional's underlying research covers 159 million trades across 29,032 US corporate bonds in the Bloomberg index universe, an unusually broad transaction-cost sample for the asset class.
insights.speaker: Aabbhas Garg, Researcher
insights.so_what: Sample breadth makes the cost-dispersion finding hard to dismiss as a small-sample or single-dealer artifact.
insights.quote: using 159 million trades across 29,032 US corporate bonds in the Bloomberg index universe

insights.claim: As of December 2024 the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index contained over 8,000 corporate issues with a market value of nearly $7 trillion, making corporate credit a large share of the investable fixed income opportunity set.
insights.speaker: Aabbhas Garg, Researcher
insights.so_what: The size of the universe is what makes substitution feasible: with 8,000+ issues there is almost always a cheaper bond with matching characteristics.
insights.locator: Corporate bonds are a significant part of the fixed income opportunity set

insights.claim: From 2013 to 2024, portfolios of low-cost US corporate bond substitutes outperformed high-cost bonds by an average of 20 bps net of transaction costs over a three-month holding period.
insights.speaker: Aabbhas Garg, Researcher
insights.so_what: A quarterly 20 bps edge is large relative to typical credit fund fees, so trading flexibility can be worth more than manager selection in this sleeve.
insights.quote: low-cost substitutes outperformed high-cost bonds by an average of 20 bps net of transaction costs, over a three-month holding period, while their gross returns are similar
insights.locator: To quantify the benefit of flexible trading

insights.claim: Because gross (mid-price) returns of high-cost bonds and their low-cost substitutes were similar, the entire performance gap is attributable to transaction costs rather than to different risk exposures or yield pickup.
insights.speaker: Aabbhas Garg, Researcher
insights.so_what: The edge is a pure cost saving, not a hidden risk premium, so it should be repeatable and does not add drawdown risk.
insights.locator: while their gross returns are similar

insights.claim: The low-cost substitution advantage held consistently across every credit quality bucket tested, including AAA–AA, A, BBB and BB.
insights.speaker: Aabbhas Garg, Researcher
insights.so_what: The effect is not concentrated in high yield or in the least liquid tier, so it applies to investment-grade mandates too.
insights.quote: This pattern is consistent across different credit quality groups (AAA–AA, A, BBB, and BB)
insights.locator: This pattern is consistent across different credit quality groups

insights.claim: The substitution test controlled for credit quality, duration and gross expected return (mid-yield), showing that cheaper bonds can be bought without altering a portfolio's intended risk exposures.
insights.speaker: Aabbhas Garg, Researcher
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete implementation rule: match on rating, duration and yield, then optimize the remaining choice on execution cost.

insights.claim: Rigid portfolio design and trading rules raise costs, a point tied to companion research on the reconstitution cost of US corporate bond indexing.
insights.speaker: Aabbhas Garg, Researcher
insights.so_what: Implicit knock on strict index-replication credit funds and ETFs that must trade specific bonds at reconstitution dates regardless of their spread cost.
insights.quote: In contrast, a lack of flexibility in portfolio design and trading can increase costs.

themes.theme: Measuring execution cost from TRACE data

insights.claim: Transaction costs in the study are estimated as the average effective spread over the prior 10 days, defined as the difference between the trade quantity-weighted customer-buy price and customer-sell price, scaled by the midpoint of those two prices.
insights.speaker: Aabbhas Garg, Researcher
insights.so_what: A replicable, pre-trade-observable cost metric investors can compute themselves to rank substitute bonds before executing.
insights.locator: Footnote 2: Transaction costs are estimated using the average effective spread

insights.claim: Mandatory FINRA TRACE reporting of over-the-counter corporate bond transactions is what makes bond-level execution cost measurable at scale for an otherwise opaque OTC market.
insights.speaker: Aabbhas Garg, Researcher
insights.so_what: Any credit manager claiming a cost edge should be able to evidence it from TRACE; ask for that evidence in due diligence.
